bullet_feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: Three stacked jargon terms up front ('EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check', 'Amazon Bedrock classifier') before the reader learns what the check is for; the payoff ('trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift') is at the very end and assumes the reader knows why retraining on a schedule is costly.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A non-engineer screener cannot restate this bullet to a hiring manager, so the strongest ML-infrastructure evidence on the page gets skipped.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'grades shift' means (the classifier's ratings drifting from the judge's?) and what problem retraining-on-demand solves
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the purpose in plain words (an automatic quality check on an AI document classifier that decides when retraining is needed), then name the mechanism; drop 'EventBridge-scheduled' to Skills or a short 'weekly/scheduled' phrase if accurate.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Designed the book as std::list FIFOs per price level inside a std::map with an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay
bullet_feedback.problem: 'std::list FIFOs per price level inside a std::map with an order-ID hash map' is a code-level data-structure description; 'O(1)' is notation a recruiter won't read. Only '1.26M events/sec' survives a non-technical read.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The recruiter can only pass along 'it was fast' and loses the design decision that is the point of the bullet; it also reads like code comments rather than a person explaining a choice.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: State the design goal in words first (orders kept in time order at each price, plus a lookup by order ID so cancels are instant), and keep the STL names short or move them to the project's tech list.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-built a research tool that scores and aggregates topics to show Amazon Leo's public-policy staff what's popular, which runs in dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code ready for production
bullet_feedback.problem: The second half ('runs in dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code ready for production') is a tool list joined by 'with'; 'runs in dev ... ready for production' is ambiguous about whether it is live. Also 'Amazon Leo' is not explained anywhere on the page.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Reader may think this is a shipped Amazon product or may assume it never launched; the tech list dilutes the one clear idea (a topic-trends tool for a policy team).
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the tool is in use by the policy staff today; what Amazon Leo is (a one-word descriptor would help)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Split into what it does for the users and one clause on deployment status; move Fargate/CDK/GitHub Actions to Skills (already listed there) unless one of them was a deliberate choice you can explain.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill's main search tool
bullet_feedback.problem: 'keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits' is unclear - it sounds like a workaround for access restrictions rather than a performance or usability win; 'category tree' is undefined.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The reason for the work reads as defensive, so the recruiter doesn't know if this was an improvement or a constraint dodge.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the permission/rate limit was blocking (the AI tool couldn't query the table directly?)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say the problem first in plain words (the AI assistant couldn't query the large table directly), then the fix (a cached, browsable catalog of popular workflows).

bullet_feedback.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost
bullet_feedback.problem: Long noun chain 'backtested Java capacity-planning logic' and 'EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching' need two reads; only one bullet under the top-billed brand.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: AWS is the first and biggest brand on the page but its only bullet is the hardest to parse in a skim, so the 7-second read lands on 'Redshift' without a takeaway.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder to plain cause then action, e.g. 'Writing Java logic that decides how much spare EC2 capacity Redshift keeps for patching, tested against historical data, to balance availability and cost.'

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
bullet_feedback.problem: Four tools stacked mid-sentence ('React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation'); 'make editing smoother' is vague next to them.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The 90% result is clear, but the eye slides over the tech list and the reader can't tell what was hard about the rebuild.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep 'desktop app with a visual drag-and-drop editor' and one or two tool names; leave the rest to Skills.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to let a vision-language model pick robot grasps for a PhD-led ICLR project, and tuned its prompts to favor grasps that avoid hitting the table
bullet_feedback.problem: 'AnyGrasp's candidate grasps' and 'Open3D' are unfamiliar names placed before the plain purpose (helping an AI choose how a robot grabs objects); 'ICLR' means nothing to most recruiters.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Recruiter skims past the only research bullet; the readable part is at the end.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Open with the goal (helping a vision-language model choose robot grasps), then the method; 'ICLR' can stay but reads better as 'a PhD-led project submitted to ICLR' if accurate.

page_feedback.problem: Section header 'UMD App Development Contracting (Client: Amazon Leo)' is ambiguous - is it a company, a university office, or a student club - and 'Amazon Leo' is not a widely known name.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: This is a third Amazon mention and potentially strong, but a recruiter can't tell its weight, so it gets discounted or flagged as a question.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Clarify the organization type in the header or title line (e.g. what 'UMD App Development Contracting' is) and add a short descriptor for Amazon Leo if space allows.

page_feedback.problem: Bolded metrics (90%, 65%, 34%, 93%, 50.9M, 12.8x, 1.26M) cluster in Capital One and the order-book project, while the AWS role at the top has no bold anchor.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: In a skim, bold sets what gets remembered; the current bolding makes the side project look like the headline over the AWS internship.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Check bolding is consistent with what you want remembered; it's fine as is if the order-book project is meant to be the headline.

page_feedback.problem: Several bullets run to the full two lines with tool lists in the middle (Capital One #1, Amazon Leo #1, EventBridge bullet), making the middle of the page dense.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The densest part of the page is where the recruiter's attention drops off, so the ML-infrastructure work is the most likely to be skipped.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Trim tool names that already appear in Technical Skills from the longest bullets.
